items.title: JetBrains/thinkrail
items.content:
Vibe code with pi in a lightweight, real IDE that customises itself around the way you work — The Vibe You Need

ThinkRail is the agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it — learning your project through living specs today, and building its own capabilities tomorrow.

We built a rich interface around the coding agent, isolated work into separate workspaces, and gave the agent durable project knowledge through living specs and reusable skills. Next, we're adding full extension support, so ThinkRail can create the tools it needs based on how you actually work.

⭐ If you find ThinkRail useful, give it a star — it helps others discover it.

A session and the change it made, scoped to an isolated git-worktree workspace.

  • Open any git repo as a project and cut workspaces from it as s, each with its own branch and working directory. Agents work in parallel without touching your checkout; merge the good branch, delete the rest. You can also attach existing worktrees or explicitly work in the project folder itself. Finished and dormant workspaces settle onto a per-project shelf on their own — when their pull request merges or closes, or after a quiet week — and come back the moment you work in them. The topbar shows where the active branch stands against and its pull request, with the next step one click away: publish, push, or open a PR described from the plan, the commits, your PR template, or an agent-written draft. Once a GitHub PR is open it shows the CI checks and review decision, and lets you mark it ready, hand failing checks or a diverged branch to the agent, merge it with the repository's last-used method, reopen it, or delete the remote branch.
  • A real IDE around the agent. A splittable workbench of Monaco editor tabs, a Files tree with live git change marks and a Changed view, terminals, and documents — all scoped to the active workspace. Leave anchored review comments on files and diffs and send them to a chat as structured context, or open the worktree in your installed IDE.
  • Chats that stream like the engine thinks. Several concurrent sessions per workspace, each with its own model and live token and cost readout. Steer a running turn or queue a follow-up, delegate to subagents, and work a shared plan the agent updates and you edit — each completed step can be committed and reviewed on its own.
  • A connected graph of files lives beside the code; the agent reads, searches, and maintains it through dedicated tools, so intent survives the session. The read-only Specs tool renders the graph as a tree in the workbench.
  • Portable Agent Skills you already keep for other coding agents are read in place, and bundled workflows guide project setup, design brainstorming, and shipping a pull request — pushing the workspace branch and opening or updating its GitHub PR through your own .
  • Agent tools beyond the shell. Web research, structured multiple-choice questions the agent asks you in the chat instead of guessing, and inline diagrams, option comparisons and file previews rendered right in the chat — when the agent proposes a UI change it shows a before/after mockup you can comment on like a diff. Settings → Extensions lists the ThinkRail extensions the agent gets and lets you switch each one off — and installs any package by source (npm, git or a local folder), for you or for a repository, showing what each one adds and letting you switch packages, their individual extensions and skills, and pi's built-ins on or off; open chats pick a change up when their turn ends. The questions and visualize tools are also published as plain packages, one each — pi install npm:@thinkrail/pi-ask-user-question for the questions (@thinkrail/pi-ask-user-question) and pi install npm:@thinkrail/pi-visualize for the diagrams and previews () — so a vanilla in the terminal gets the same tools.
  • Connect the MCP servers in your (or add them, and a few presets, from Settings): ThinkRail asks in the chat before calls the server does not mark read-only (or always allows the tools you trust in a project), keeps servers a repository defines off until you approve them, signs you in to OAuth servers from Settings, and shows each chat's servers next to its background commands and subagents.
  • Your providers, your credentials. Sign in with JetBrains AI or connect any provider through 's own auth. ThinkRail has no accounts of its own.
  • ThinkRail reads your existing configuration (). To use another one — say a personal — or to pass extra environment variables to the agent, terminals and MCP servers, set them in Settings → Environment; they apply on the next start. A variable you set when launching (PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=… thinkrail) still wins.
  • Settings → Providers → connects a company LLM gateway or a model running on your own machine — any OpenAI-compatible server, such as LiteLLM, sglang, vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp. lists what the server serves, with the context and capabilities it reports. The server is saved to 's , so its models appear in the chat model picker and in the CLI alike.
  • A native desktop app, or the CLI that opens the same app in your browser. Both embed the same engine host; app state lives under .
  • Settings → Language follows your system language or a language you pick; English, Japanese, Russian, Simplified Chinese, and Spanish are built in. Add a language ThinkRail doesn't ship yet by dropping a translated into — it applies as you save. Agent replies and tool output stay as the agent wrote them.
  • Settings → Appearance ships dark, light, minimal and high-contrast themes. Make your own by copying a bundled , changing its id and colors, and saving it to .
  • Settings → Appearance picks the interface and code fonts from the bundled Geist and JetBrains Mono, any font installed on your computer, or font files you drop in (kept in ), with fallback fonts for icon glyphs, a code size, ligatures and a text-weight slider.

The project's spec graph as a tree, with the spec itself rendered alongside.

ThinkRail ships in two additive forms: a native desktop installer and the self-contained CLI. Both are published with on the releases page.

Download the asset for your platform:

  • macOS 14+ (Apple Silicon or Intel) — open the DMG for your architecture: thinkrail-desktop-darwin-arm64.dmg or thinkrail-desktop-darwin-x64.dmg.

  • — extract the complete setup ZIP, then run its setup executable in place, next to its payload.

  • — extract the setup tarball and run . Desktop builds need glibc 2.38+ with GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, Ayatana AppIndicator 3, and librsvg 2 — Ubuntu 24.04 or newer:

    sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2

Packaged stable and nightly desktop builds check for updates in the background and offer them in : → → . Nothing is applied until you choose . ThinkRail then shows the installation's progress and log, closes, and reopens on the new version. After the restart it tells you whether the update installed. If it didn't, it explains why and offers to retry. The updater appears only when the package carries a valid HTTPS feed identity; installations that predate that identity need one manual installation first.

The installer downloads the right binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and puts on your PATH.

(also Windows under Git Bash):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash

— the same command works from cmd and PowerShell:

powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex"

Then run , optionally with a git repo to open as a project:

needs on your PATH and a model provider — sign in with JetBrains AI from the app or use your own provider credentials. The first launch walks you through connecting a provider and picking a project; creates an empty git repository (under by default), so you don't need one ready. Add project → Clone repository… clones a Git URL into a new folder on the computer running ThinkRail and opens it as a project. Choose the parent folder and folder name, optionally limit the history depth, or cancel an in-progress clone. GitHub and other Git hosts work with the host's existing Git credentials and SSH keys; existing destination folders are never overwritten. lists the flags; prints the build.

macOS Apple Silicon / Intel
signed setup executable and app binaries

JetBrains signs the Windows CLI, the desktop setup executable, and every executable and DLL the desktop app installs. The macOS CLI is signed but not yet notarized. Signed and notarized desktop DMGs require the coordinated JetBrains service pipeline; older published DMGs and locally built packages may still be unsigned and blocked by Gatekeeper. Linux artifacts are unsigned.

ThinkRail apps collect basic usage events — launches, chat creation, message sends, provider connections — tied to a random installation ID. Usage analytics never include prompts, code, files, credentials, or account identity. Error reports are also always sent, tied to the same installation ID, so we can fix crashes: the error type and code and where in ThinkRail's own code it happened. They never include error messages, file paths, names, URLs, or anything from your projects or extensions. Additional product usage and how you found ThinkRail are shared only while Share additional usage data is on; the switch is offered as a step of first-run setup (or right after you skip it) and lives in . When launching from the command line, (or ) turns additional sharing off for that run. With additional sharing on, a packaged build may open the ThinkRail blog in your browser once to link your installation to the website visit that brought you here — only where you accepted marketing cookies on the website or no consent is required — and that link expires after 30 days.

Feedback surveys are separate from usage analytics. ThinkRail may invite you to a short survey, and you can also open it from . Your answers, including anything you type, are sent to the ThinkRail team only when you press , whatever your analytics settings, and are tied to the same random installation ID — not to your name or account. Please don't include secrets, code, or personal data; to have your answers deleted, email info@thinkrail.ai.

The ThinkRail apps and the ThinkRail website (thinkrail.ai) use PostHog Inc. services for analytics. The website also uses PostHog Surveys to collect feedback after a desktop download and, only if you choose to enter one, your email address, which is used to ask for further feedback and to send product updates. PostHog's privacy policy is at posthog.com/privacy.

ThinkRail is a thin host that runs in-process and bridges it to a rich web UI. owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state; the app owns the workspace, the editor, and the wire — it never assembles prompts behind your back. Three rings:

  • — (+ ): a HTTP+WS host with one in-process session per chat, launched by or .
  • — : the typed, versioned protocol between host and UI.
  • — : React 19 + Zustand + Tailwind v4, shipped independently; it dials a host over the wire and depends on the contracts only.

and are the canonical product and design specs. ThinkRail is developed spec-first: a sits beside every module, and a change that moves a boundary, contract, or decision updates the spec in the same change.

You need 1.4.4 (the pinned package manager and runtime), ≥ 22.19 (required by the in-process engine), and an authenticated provider for agent work.

git clone https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail.git
cd thinkrail
bun install
bun run dev                          # host + web client together; Ctrl+C stops both

bun run --filter @thinkrail/cli dev  # browser launcher
bun run build:binary                 # standalone CLI artifact
bun run desktop:dev                  # package and open the Electrobun app
bun run desktop:build                # package without opening it

covers the checks, the end-to-end suites, desktop packaging, and the repository layout.

Join us on Discord to ask questions, share what you're building, and talk to the team. Bugs and feature requests go to GitHub issues.

items.title: TauricResearch/TradingAgents
items.content:
TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework

  • [2026-10] released with runs on your own ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan, backtests scored from the first close after each decision, a note at start-up when a newer release is out, and a wheel attached to each GitHub release.
  • [2026-10] released with reports saved as one HTML page, a provider per model tier so the managers and analysts can run on different models, past decisions settled for every ticker while the analysts work, and company news read from Yahoo search while Yahoo's news feed is down.
  • [2026-09] released with parallel analysts for a faster analysis, a CLI that runs without prompts from flags such as and , the run's settings recorded in every report, and backtests that see only data published by each analysis date.

🎉 officially released! We have received numerous inquiries about the work, and we would like to express our thanks for the enthusiasm in our community.

So we decided to fully open-source the framework. Looking forward to building impactful projects with you!

TradingAgents is a multi-agent trading framework that mirrors the dynamics of real-world trading firms. By deploying specialized LLM-powered agents: from fundamental analysts, sentiment experts, and technical analysts, to trader, risk management team, the platform collaboratively evaluates market conditions and informs trading decisions. Moreover, these agents engage in dynamic discussions to pinpoint the optimal strategy.

Our framework decomposes complex trading tasks into specialized roles.

  • Fundamentals Analyst: Evaluates company financials and performance metrics, identifying intrinsic values and potential red flags.
  • Sentiment Analyst: Aggregates news headlines, StockTwits, and Reddit chatter into a single sentiment read to gauge short-term market mood.
  • News Analyst: Monitors global news and macroeconomic indicators, interpreting the impact of events on market conditions.
  • Technical Analyst: Utilizes technical indicators (like MACD and RSI) to detect trading patterns and forecast price movements.

The selected analysts work at the same time, each on its own tools, and the research debate starts once all of their reports are in.

  • Comprises both bullish and bearish researchers who critically assess the insights provided by the Analyst Team. Through structured debates, they balance potential gains against inherent risks.
  • Composes reports from the analysts and researchers to make informed trading decisions, determining the timing and magnitude of trades.

Risk Management and Portfolio Manager

  • Continuously evaluates portfolio risk by assessing market volatility, liquidity, and other risk factors. The risk management team evaluates and adjusts trading strategies, providing assessment reports to the Portfolio Manager for final decision.
  • The Portfolio Manager approves/rejects the transaction proposal. If approved, the order will be sent to the simulated exchange and executed.
git clone https://github.com/TauricResearch/TradingAgents.git
cd TradingAgents

TradingAgents needs Python 3.11 or later. Create a virtual environment in any of your favorite environment managers:

conda create -n tradingagents python=3.13
conda activate tradingagents

uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate

Install the package and its dependencies ( with uv):

Alternatively, run with Docker:

cp .env.example .env  # add your API keys
docker compose run --rm tradingagents

After updating the repository, rebuild the image with .

Results, reports, the memory log and the cache live in the volume. To keep them in a folder on the host instead, create the folder and point at it, in or the shell: mkdir -p data && TRADINGAGENTS_DATA_DIR=./data docker compose run --rm tradingagents.

For local models with Ollama:

docker compose --profile ollama run --rm tradingagents-ollama

TradingAgents supports multiple LLM providers. Set the API key for your chosen provider:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=...          # OpenAI (GPT)
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=...          # Google (Gemini)
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...       # Anthropic (Claude)
export XAI_API_KEY=...             # xAI (Grok)
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...        # DeepSeek
export DASHSCOPE_API_KEY=...       # Qwen (international, dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com)
export DASHSCOPE_CN_API_KEY=...    # Qwen (China, dashscope.aliyuncs.com)
export ZHIPU_API_KEY=...           # GLM via Z.AI (international)
export ZHIPU_CN_API_KEY=...        # GLM via BigModel (China, open.bigmodel.cn)
export MINIMAX_API_KEY=...         # MiniMax (global, api.minimax.io)
export MINIMAX_CN_API_KEY=...      # MiniMax (China, api.minimaxi.com)
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...      # OpenRouter
export MISTRAL_API_KEY=...         # Mistral
export MOONSHOT_API_KEY=...        # Kimi (Moonshot)
export GROQ_API_KEY=...            # Groq
export NVIDIA_API_KEY=...          # NVIDIA NIM
export FRED_API_KEY=...            # FRED macro data (free, optional)
export ALPHA_VANTAGE_API_KEY=...   # Alpha Vantage
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...        # Jev social-post screening (optional)

For Azure OpenAI, copy to and fill in your credentials.

To run on your ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan instead of an API key, choose "Subscription" in the CLI's provider menu, or set . Sign in once with tradingagents login chatgpt: it prints an address to open in your browser, which returns to this machine on . When the browser runs on another machine, or TradingAgents runs in Docker (docker compose run --rm tradingagents login chatgpt), paste the address the browser ends up on. The sign-in is kept in ~/.tradingagents/chatgpt-auth.json, and tradingagents logout chatgpt revokes it. Runs count toward your plan's usage limits, and the plan does not accept or .

For AWS Bedrock, install the extra with , set , configure AWS credentials (environment variables, , or an IAM role) and , and use a Bedrock model ID, e.g. us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5.

For local models, configure Ollama with . The default endpoint is http://localhost:11434/v1; set to point at a remote . Pull models with , and pick "Custom model ID" in the CLI for any model not listed by default.

For any other OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, LM Studio, llama.cpp, or a custom relay), use llm_provider: "openai_compatible" and set the endpoint via (or TRADINGAGENTS_LLM_BACKEND_URL), e.g. for vLLM or for LM Studio. The model is whatever your server serves. No key is needed for local servers; set OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY when the endpoint requires one.

With set, the Sentiment Analyst screens StockTwits and Reddit posts with TypeSafe's Jev before reading them. Posts that are not about the company are dropped, and each source opens with a count of the remaining posts by stance: bullish, bearish, neutral, or unclear. Without the key, posts pass through unscreened. moves with new releases; set to a versioned ID such as to hold it fixed across runs. To reach Jev through OpenRouter, put an OpenRouter key in and set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api.

Alternatively, copy to and fill in your keys:

Launch the interactive CLI:

tradingagents          # installed command
python -m cli.main     # alternative: run directly from source

You will see a screen where you can select your desired tickers, analysis date, LLM provider, research depth, and more. Your previous run's answers come back as the defaults, so pressing Enter accepts them. The variables in still skip their step entirely.

To run without questions, for a scheduled job or a script, answer the per-run steps with flags and the rest with variables:

export TRADINGAGENTS_LLM_PROVIDER=openai TRADINGAGENTS_QUICK_THINK_LLM=gpt-6-luna TRADINGAGENTS_DEEP_THINK_LLM=gpt-6-sol
export TRADINGAGENTS_OUTPUT_LANGUAGE=English TRADINGAGENTS_MAX_DEBATE_ROUNDS=1 TRADINGAGENTS_MAX_RISK_ROUNDS=1
tradingagents --ticker NVDA --date 2026-09-23 --analysts market,news,fundamentals --save --no-show

Each flag skips only its own question. Run without a terminal, a missing answer stops the run before it starts and names the flag or variable to set.

At start-up the interactive CLI mentions a newer release and notices from Tauric Research. It checks at most once a day, in the background, and sends nothing about your runs; set TRADINGAGENTS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to turn it off. Runs without a terminal never check.

A saved report also includes , the report as one page with its sections listed beside the text, for reading in a browser, on a phone or in print. Answering the save question at the prompt also asks about the page and can open it in your browser; skips it, and so does ta.save_reports(state, "NVDA", html=False) from Python.

TradingAgents works with any market Yahoo Finance covers, using the exchange-suffixed ticker. Company identity and the alpha benchmark resolve automatically per market.

  • Hong Kong: · Tokyo: · London:
  • India: , · Canada: · Australia:
  • China A-shares: Shanghai , Shenzhen (e.g. for Kweichow Moutai)

An interface will appear showing results as they load, letting you track the agent's progress as it runs.

We built TradingAgents with LangGraph to ensure flexibility and modularity. The framework supports multiple LLM providers: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen (Alibaba DashScope, international and China endpoints), GLM (Zhipu), MiniMax (global + China), OpenRouter, Ollama for local models, Azure OpenAI for enterprise, and your own ChatGPT plan.

To use TradingAgents inside your code, you can import the module and initialize a object. The function will return a decision. You can run , here's also a quick example:

from tradingagents.graph.trading_graph import TradingAgentsGraph
from tradingagents.default_config import DEFAULT_CONFIG

ta = TradingAgentsGraph(debug=True, config=DEFAULT_CONFIG.copy())

# forward propagate
state, decision = ta.propagate("NVDA", "2026-09-01")
print(decision)

# the same report tree the CLI saves, under results_dir/reports
ta.save_reports(state, "NVDA")

You can also adjust the default configuration to set your own choice of LLMs, debate rounds, etc.

from tradingagents.graph.trading_graph import TradingAgentsGraph
from tradingagents.default_config import DEFAULT_CONFIG

config = DEFAULT_CONFIG.copy()
config["llm_provider"] = "openai"        # e.g. openai, google, anthropic, deepseek, groq, ollama; openai_compatible covers any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, LM Studio, llama.cpp, ...)
config["deep_think_llm"] = "gpt-6-sol"    # Model for complex reasoning
config["quick_think_llm"] = "gpt-6-luna"   # Model for quick tasks
config["max_debate_rounds"] = 2

ta = TradingAgentsGraph(debug=True, config=config)
_, decision = ta.propagate("NVDA", "2026-09-01")
print(decision)

The quick model serves the analysts, researchers, debaters and trader; the deep model serves the research and portfolio managers. Each can run on its own provider, for example the managers on Claude while the rest run on OpenAI:

config["deep_think_provider"] = "anthropic"
config["deep_think_llm"] = "claude-opus-5-5"

A tier on its own provider uses that provider's key and default endpoint; set or for a local or relay endpoint. The TRADINGAGENTS_DEEP_THINK_PROVIDER and TRADINGAGENTS_QUICK_THINK_PROVIDER variables set them for the CLI, together with the tier's model variable.

See tradingagents/default_config.py for all configuration options.

US company statements come from SEC EDGAR, which records the date every figure was filed. A run dated in the past reads the statements exactly as they stood that day: a fiscal year that has ended but has not been filed yet is not served, and a figure restated later still reads as first reported. Apple's 2008 total assets were filed as $39.6B and restated to $36.2B in 2010, so a run dated in between reads $39.6B. EDGAR needs no account or API key.

Other companies' statements come from Yahoo Finance, which dates a statement by the period it covers rather than by when it was published. A run dated today reads them; a run dated in the past is told they are withheld, since Yahoo cannot say which figures were public by then.

Insider trades are dated by when they happened, not when they were filed, so a run dated in the past is told they are withheld as well.

SEC asks callers to identify themselves and refuses requests that carry no contact address, so a default one is sent. Set your own so SEC can reach you rather than the project:

SEC_EDGAR_USER_AGENT="Your Name your@email.com"

It covers companies that file with the SEC, including foreign companies listed in the US. Anything else, such as Hong Kong or A-share listings, falls through to the next vendor in the chain. EDGAR's machine-readable filings begin in 2009, and a fourth quarter is reported as unavailable rather than derived, because filers publish it only inside the annual figure.

By default the agents do not know what you hold, so their guidance is written for a reader who applies it to their own position. Pass a portfolio to have the trader, the risk analysts and the portfolio manager work against your actual book.

from tradingagents.portfolio import PortfolioContext

portfolio = PortfolioContext.model_validate({
    "cash": 25000.0,
    "currency": "USD",
    "positions": [{"ticker": "NVDA", "quantity": 120, "average_price": 150.0}],
})
_, decision = ta.propagate("NVDA", "2026-09-01", portfolio=portfolio)

The CLI takes the same content as a JSON file: tradingagents --portfolio my_book.json.

An empty list means a flat book, which is different from passing nothing. A run without a portfolio is never treated as flat.

TradingAgents persists two kinds of state across runs.

The memory log is always on. Each completed run appends its decision to ~/.tradingagents/memory/trading_memory.md. While the analysts of a later run work, TradingAgents settles every logged decision whose holding period has passed: it fetches the realised return (raw, and alpha against the instrument's regional benchmark) and generates a one-paragraph reflection. The Portfolio Manager then reads the most recent decisions for the same ticker plus recent lessons from other tickers, so each analysis carries forward what worked and what didn't. If settling fails, the run goes on and its report says so.

Override the path with TRADINGAGENTS_MEMORY_LOG_PATH.

To settle decisions without running an analysis, for a scheduled job, call ; it returns the decisions it settled and any it could not.

Checkpoint resume is opt-in via . When enabled, LangGraph saves state after each node so a crashed or interrupted run resumes from the last successful step instead of starting over. The run view says whether it resumed a saved run or started fresh. Checkpoints are cleared automatically on successful completion.

Per-ticker SQLite databases live at ~/.tradingagents/cache/checkpoints/<TICKER>.db (override the base with ). Use to reset all of them before a run.

tradingagents --checkpoint           # enable for this run
tradingagents --clear-checkpoints    # reset before running

config = DEFAULT_CONFIG.copy()
config["checkpoint_enabled"] = True
ta = TradingAgentsGraph(config=config)
_, decision = ta.propagate("NVDA", "2026-09-01")

Evaluating decisions over time

One run gives one decision, which cannot tell you whether the system decides well. runs the same pipeline over a grid of tickers and dates, writes to a memory log of its own, and scores the decisions whose holding window has since traded.

from tradingagents.backtest import iter_grid, run_backtest, summarize

dates = iter_grid("2026-06-01", "2026-08-01", every_n_days=7)
result = run_backtest(["NVDA", "AAPL"], dates, config, selected_analysts=["market", "news"])
print(summarize(result).render())

tradingagents backtest NVDA,AAPL --start 2026-06-01 --end 2026-08-01 --every 7

Each cell is scored on realized alpha against the instrument's regional benchmark, grouped by rating. A decision is entered at the first close after its date, because a run reads news published after that day's close. Your own memory log is never written to, and re-running the same grid with skips the cells that already ran, so an interrupted sweep continues where it stopped.

TradingAgents is LLM-driven, so two runs of the same ticker and date can differ. This is expected for a research tool built on language models, not a defect. The variation comes from a few distinct sources, and it helps to separate them.

Language model sampling is non-deterministic. Even at a fixed temperature, providers do not guarantee byte-identical output across calls, and reasoning models (the default GPT-6 family, and any thinking-mode model) vary the most because their internal reasoning is itself sampled.

Live data moves. News, StockTwits, and Reddit return different content as time passes, so a run today sees different inputs than a run last week even for the same historical trade date. Pin the analysis date to hold the price and indicator window fixed, but the social and news sources still reflect "now".

To reduce variation you can lower the sampling temperature. Set in your config (or TRADINGAGENTS_TEMPERATURE in ); lower values make models that honor it more repeatable. The current curated models are reasoning-first and largely ignore temperature, so for tighter reproducibility name a non-reasoning model in your config, or in TRADINGAGENTS_DEEP_THINK_LLM and TRADINGAGENTS_QUICK_THINK_LLM. Any model ID your provider serves is accepted, whether or not the picker lists it.

config = DEFAULT_CONFIG.copy()
config["llm_provider"] = "openai"
config["temperature"] = 0.0
# Reasoning models ignore temperature. For tighter reproducibility, name a
# non-reasoning model in deep_think_llm / quick_think_llm.

What does not vary anymore: the analyzed company identity is resolved deterministically from the ticker before any agent runs, and the market analyst grounds exact price and indicator claims in a verified data snapshot. Earlier reports of "different companies" or fabricated price levels across runs are addressed by these two mechanisms.

Backtest results are not guaranteed to match any published figure. Returns depend on the model, the temperature, the date range, data quality, and the sampling above. Treat the framework as a research scaffold for studying multi-agent analysis, not as a strategy with a fixed, replicable return.

Contributions are welcome: bug fixes, documentation, and feature ideas; past contributions are credited per release in .

Please reference our work if you find provides you with some help 😃

@misc{xiao2025tradingagentsmultiagentsllmfinancial,
      title={TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework}, 
      author={Yijia Xiao and Edward Sun and Di Luo and Wei Wang},
      year={2025},
      eprint={2412.20138},
      archivePrefix={arXiv},
      primaryClass={q-fin.TR},
      url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20138}, 
}

items.title: makecindy/cindy
items.content:
Consider it done. The open-source AI agent that works out of the box · 想到，就能做到。开源、开箱即用的 AI Agent。

Cindy is an open-source AI agent, ready out of the box and yours to shape. Connect your computers and phone, bring the models and subscriptions you already use, and build a companion that knows how you like to work.

All your devices. One Cindy.

Your work computer, home desktop, laptop and phone belong together.

  • Open a session from another device, continue the conversation, and access its files without copying everything into a new chat.
  • Share more than a screen. Use model providers configured on another computer — including supported subscriptions, API providers and local models.
  • Reach your whole desktop. Built-in remote desktop on your phone lets you open apps, type and operate a connected computer when a chat isn't enough.

Your computer becomes your server: no server rental or self-hosting setup.

Keep your favorite agents. Get a better way to work.

Already using Claude Code or Codex? Cindy brings them together with , then adds a shared interface, multi-device access, tools and a companion of your own.

Claude Code's agent workflow, with Cindy's interface and connected tools.
Codex's coding workflow, available alongside your other agents.
A lean, open-source, extensible agent with support for multiple model providers.

Choose a supported harness and model combination, and change it as the work evolves. Your session stays in Cindy; switching harnesses hands off or rebuilds the engine context rather than making their internal states identical.

One agent not enough? Let her lead a team. Use different agents for planning, parallel implementation and independent review, with a shared goal and clear acceptance criteria.

Real work, in your actual tools

Work with your files, browser and apps. Ask for a change, inspect what happened, and keep working from the result. Answers can include charts, interactive controls and rich HTML, not just a wall of text.

Build a recurring routine with , or hand over work through connected chat channels such as Slack and Telegram. Connect more tools through .

Ready from day one. Yours to shape over time.

  • Create your own companions. Give them a role, instructions, skills and recurring work — a reviewer, researcher, project partner, or something of your own.
  • Make experience reusable. Keep useful preferences and knowledge in memory; turn a good way of working into a Skill you can reuse and share.
  • Discover Skills and plugins in SkillHub, connect your own tools, or build on the official plugins.
  • Audit the code, fork it, improve an interaction, fix a bug, or contribute a useful integration. The client is Apache-2.0 licensed.

Start with what you already have

The . Authorize a supported subscription you already pay for, including Claude Code or Codex plans, connect your own API keys, or use a local model. You can also use Cindy's managed model service. Provider limits and billing still apply; the free client does not mean unlimited model usage.

macOS · Windows · Linux · iOS · Android

This repository contains Cindy's open-source desktop and mobile clients and their shared packages, organized as a pnpm monorepo.

Expo / React Native mobile client
Shared client capabilities (auth, device-link, agent orchestration, model providers, …)
Tool binaries shipped with the desktop app; none are committed — claude-code, codex, and ripgrep are downloaded per platform by , and the Android platform-tools binaries are fetched (pinned version, sha256-verified) before Windows packaging

the backend service lives in a separate repository and is not part of this monorepo.

Use Cindy's full hosted service. See pricing.
No Cindy sign-in requiredChoose “Skip Sign-In” on the login screen to use local agents; the app then shows the account state as “Not signed in”. Server-backed capabilities are unavailable in this state.
  • 10.x (v11 is not yet supported)

Contributor setup, Git LFS, dependency updates, and access requirements are maintained in . Plugins are installed through SkillHub or manually.

git clone https://github.com/makecindy/cindy.git
cd cindy
git lfs pull
pnpm install

# Mainland China Cindy account
pnpm restart:desktop:remote --region=cn

# Global Cindy account
pnpm restart:desktop:remote --region=global

Remote development uses your own Cindy cloud account and existing login state, so you can continue existing sessions and work while developing the client. Use for Mainland China accounts and for everyone else; do not rely on the internal default. Full desktop, mobile, data-isolation, and validation workflows are in .

“Skip Sign-In” on the login screen runs local agents without a Cindy account (shown in the app as “Not signed in”), not a connection to a local server. Server-backed capabilities are unavailable in this state.

About the default servers: the client connects to Cindy's official cloud services by default (endpoint manifests in and config/endpoint.global.json; desktop auto-updates also come from the official CDN). This is intentional — external developers don't need to self-host a server: sign in with your own Cindy account in a dev build and develop / test directly against the official servers.

Skill Hub migration uses two separate manifest fields: released clients keep using (the deprecated XD proxy), while current clients use . The current client deliberately does not fall back to the legacy field when the new endpoint is absent.

Never commit credentials or authorization files to the working tree. If you discover a security issue, follow to report it privately rather than opening a public issue.

Official distribution builds include TapDB usage analytics for product-level aggregate statistics, including device identifiers, OS / app version, startup and activity events. Events are associated with your account ID after sign-in, so this is not fully anonymous. TapDB does collect chat content, file content, or working-directory data.

You can disable usage analytics without editing code: on Desktop, use Settings → About → Usage statistics; on Mobile, use Usage statistics in Settings. The SDK checks the stored privacy-consent state and the statistics preference, which defaults to on. Accepting the Privacy Policy records consent; a one-time migration also records consent for eligible existing signed-in users.

enterprise SSO skips the policy-acceptance step. If no analytics consent record exists and that sign-in is restored after restarting the app, the current migration can mark even a new installation as consented. With TapDB configured and statistics enabled, reporting can then start without explicit policy acceptance. See Mobile sign-in restoration and the consent migration. Turning off Usage statistics prevents reporting from being enabled by this migration.

  • Desktop stops subsequent analytics reporting immediately when disabled. Local mode (Skip sign-in) does not report to TapDB.
  • Mobile immediately unlinks the account and stops reports explicitly triggered by Cindy. An already initialized native SDK cannot be uninitialized; fully quit and relaunch the app to keep the SDK uninitialized.

Online heartbeats and diagnostic logs are separate mechanisms, unaffected by the usage statistics switch. Desktop sends heartbeats to Cindy services only during a verified cloud sign-in (account ID, platform, and version); local mode sends none. Desktop native crash dumps stay local and are never uploaded automatically. Diagnostic logs can be uploaded manually; a separate, default-off automatic crash log upload option is also available. Log uploads require privacy consent. See the heartbeat implementation and log upload rules.

You are not required to keep analytics:

  • Desktop development builds do not initialize TapDB by default. Explicitly setting lifts the build gate but still requires consent and the statistics preference. Self-packaged Desktop builds use the same analytics gates as official builds; you can disable analytics in Settings.
  • Mobile does not initialize the SDK without injected TapDB configuration ( / ). This does not mean all source builds default to off: the self-hosted release pipeline requires nonempty configuration, while local development permits empty values. See the Mobile build guide.

Except as otherwise noted, the source code in this repository is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. Individual source files do not carry per-file license headers; the repository-root governs.

Model weights, datasets, prompts, trademarks, and other separately identified materials may be subject to their own license terms and are not automatically covered by the repository-level Apache-2.0 grant. Third-party open-source components retain their own copyright and license. Their attribution notices and SPDX SBOMs are managed under , with artifact-specific outputs in . See for this project's copyright and attribution information.

items.title: google-gemini/gemini-cli
items.content:
An open-source AI agent that brings the power of Gemini directly into your terminal.

Unpaid tier and Google One users: Gemini CLI was replaced by Antigravity CLI on June 18th, 2026. To learn more, see our blog post.

Gemini CLI has not been optimized for Gemini 4 Argon. To use Gemini 4 Argon, please use Antigravity.

Gemini CLI is not optimized for the latest Gemini models. For the best coding experience with Gemini models use Antigravity CLI

Gemini CLI is an open-source AI agent that brings the power of Gemini directly into your terminal. It provides lightweight access to Gemini, giving you the most direct path from your prompt to our model.

# Using npx (no installation required)
npx @google/gemini-cli

Install globally with npm

npm install -g @google/gemini-cli

Install globally with Homebrew (macOS/Linux)

Install globally with MacPorts (macOS)

sudo port install gemini-cli

Install with Anaconda (for restricted environments)

# Create and activate a new environment
conda create -y -n gemini_env -c conda-forge nodejs
conda activate gemini_env

# Install Gemini CLI globally via npm (inside the environment)
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli

New preview releases will be published each week at UTC 23:59 on Tuesdays. These releases will not have been fully vetted and may contain regressions or other outstanding issues. Please help us test and install with tag.

npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@preview
  • New stable releases will be published each week at UTC 20:00 on Tuesdays, this will be the full promotion of last week's release + any bug fixes and validations. Use tag.
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@latest
  • New releases will be published each day at UTC 00:00. This will be all changes from the main branch as represented at time of release. It should be assumed there are pending validations and issues. Use tag.
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@nightly

Code Understanding & Generation

  • Query and edit large codebases
  • Generate new apps from PDFs, images, or sketches using multimodal capabilities
  • Debug issues and troubleshoot with natural language
  • Automate operational tasks like querying pull requests or handling complex rebases
  • Run non-interactively in scripts for workflow automation

Choose the authentication method that best fits your needs:

Option 1: Sign in with Google (OAuth login using your Google Account)

When using a paid Code Assist License from your organization, remember to set the Google Cloud Project

# Set your Google Cloud Project
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
gemini

Developers who need specific model control or paid tier access

  • : Upgrade for higher limits when needed
# Get your key from https://aistudio.google.com/apikey
export GEMINI_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY"
gemini

Enterprise teams and production workloads

  • : Higher rate limits with billing account
  • : Works with existing Google Cloud infrastructure
# Get your key from Google Cloud Console
export GOOGLE_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY"
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=true
gemini

Gemini CLI is not optimized for the latest Gemini models. For the best coding experience with Gemini models use Antigravity CLI

Start in current directory

Include multiple directories

gemini --include-directories ../lib,../docs

gemini -m gemini-2.5-flash

Non-interactive mode for scripts

Get a simple text response:

For more advanced scripting, including how to parse JSON and handle errors, use the flag to get structured output:

For real-time event streaming (useful for monitoring long-running operations), use --output-format stream-json to get newline-delimited JSON events:

Troubleshooting & Support

Configure MCP servers in to extend Gemini CLI with custom tools:

> @github List my open pull requests
> @slack Send a summary of today's commits to #dev channel

We welcome contributions! Gemini CLI is fully open source (Apache 2.0), and we encourage the community to:

  • Report bugs and suggest features.

items.title: pollen-robotics/microduck
items.content:
A Tiny biped duck robot 🦆

A tiny biped robot that moves using reinforcement learning policies.

This repo is the duck's brain. About 25 cm and 800 g of robot, run by a handful of daemons on a Rockchip RK3566: a 50 Hz control loop driving fifteen servos from neural policies, the radios and the camera, and the update machinery that gets new software onto a robot without bricking it.

Everything you need to run a Microduck is here.

The policies it runs are trained next door, in — MuJoCo and PPO, the sim2real recipe, and the export to ONNX that this repo loads.

Pick up a gamepad and drive. Put wheels on, ask for roller mode, and it loads the other brain.
Beak to the floor, one button. Knock it over and it stands itself up.

It also sits, kicks a ball, rolls forward on command, and quacks in a voice that is its own.

Every command: drive, configure, voice, chorale, theremin, wifi, updates, logs. Start here.
The full button mapping, and pairing a pad — once per pad, plus what to do when it will not bond.
The robot from a laptop over Bluetooth, with no network and no ssh.
Install, roll back, pin. Every update is verified, health-gated and reversible.
Where the policies come from: MuJoCo, PPO, domain randomisation, and the ONNX export this repo loads.
The whole system on one page — the daemons, the bus, how an update reaches a robot — then a page per part.
Branch builds, release candidates, driving from a laptop, and the restart traps after an update.
No robot on the desk? runs the real daemons against a body in MuJoCo — one duck in a window, or four as machines you log into.
Everything, including the design pages and the open problems.

Rust, no framework, one workspace. owns the control loop and the motor bus; installs signed releases and rolls them back when a robot comes up unhealthy; owns wifi and identity; is the Bluetooth path a phone uses; reads the gamepad; streams the camera over WebRTC; serves the depth sensor. They talk over one JSON-RPC contract on Unix sockets, and every client — the app, the console, the gamepad, your script — sends exactly the same calls.

The interesting decisions are written down: is why things are the way they are, and is what has gone wrong and what would close it.

No duck was harmed in the making of this robot. Several were consulted.

items.title: pbakaus/impeccable
items.content:
The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.

The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with and , review with and , and catch AI slop before it ships.

Reload your coding tool, then run in your agent ( on Codex).

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Replit Agent, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, Kiro, Trae, Rovo Dev, Qoder, Mistral Vibe, Pi, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek Harness, and Veto. Full docs live at impeccable.style/docs.

Same model (Fable 5.1), same brief: a fourteen-room family guesthouse on the Ligurian coast. Without Impeccable, it builds the tasteful default: cream page, thin serif, italic accent, pill buttons. With it, the page is built around one picture: the house at night, seen from the water.

For a full project, see the Neo Mirai case study: a conference site taken from mockup to shipped page.

Inter for everything. Purple-to-blue gradients. Cards nested in cards, gray text on colored backgrounds, a rounded-square icon tile above every heading. Ask an agent for a page with no other guidance and these show up again and again, across models and projects.

  • "Make it pop" leaves your agent to guess. /impeccable bolder the pricing cards loads a playbook written for that one move and points it at one target.
  • scores the design against usability heuristics and ranks what to fix first. checks accessibility, performance, theming, and responsive behavior, with findings ranked P0 (blocking) to P3 (polish).
  • 62 deterministic rules flag the tells above, plus quality problems like cramped padding and skipped headings. No LLM, no API key.

Impeccable is strongest on interfaces that already exist: point it at a page or a component and iterate. It builds new pages too; see Build something new for how to get the most out of that harder mode. To start, pick one component:

/impeccable critique the pricing cards

Run once per project. It reads your code, asks only what it can't infer (who the product is for, what it needs to do, the constraints), and writes . Every later command reads it. Run to capture your existing visual system in , so changes stay on-brand. More on context files.

Then name a command and a target:

/impeccable critique the onboarding flow
/impeccable quieter the landing page
/impeccable polish settings
/impeccable harden checkout

Or just describe what you want: /impeccable redo this hero section. Narrow targets get better results; a single section reviewed closely beats a whole page at a glance. Pin a command you use often with to get as its own shortcut.

amplifies safe designs · tones down loud ones · removes what the page doesn't need · brings color to a gray interface · fixes fonts, hierarchy, and sizing · fixes spacing and rhythm · adds transitions and interaction feedback · adds personality · goes for shaders, spring physics, and scroll-driven effects
is a scored UX review · is a technical quality report
is the final pass before shipping · covers errors, i18n, overflow, and edge cases · rewrites unclear copy · handles screen sizes and devices · fixes loading and rendering performance · designs first-run flows and empty states
lets you pick an element in the browser and cycle through variants · produces variants of a named element without manual picking
plans UX before code · writes · writes · pulls repeated patterns into your design system

The 24th, , is a deprecated alias for a plain build request. Type alone to see the list in your agent. Each command has its own page: impeccable.style/docs.

On Codex, open or type instead of the slash command.

opens your running dev server with an overlay. Select an element, pick a direction, and Impeccable hot-swaps variants in place. Accept one and it is written back to your source. It works with Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML. Iterate in the browser.

Live mode edits a local checkout only; don't inject it into a deployed site or weaken a production CSP to make it work. Applying copy edits runs your 's optional impeccable:manual-edit-validate script with your permissions, so review it before using live mode in an unfamiliar repo.

Three ways to run the detector

The design hook scans every UI file your agent edits and hands the findings back before the agent calls the work done. This is where most slop gets caught: without the hook, the detector only runs when someone remembers to run it. It's available on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, and Hermes Agent, and the installer sets it up. Say yes. Automatic design checks.

The CLI needs no agent:

npx impeccable detect src/                   # scan a directory
npx impeccable detect https://example.com    # scan a rendered page (uses your installed Chrome or Edge)
npx impeccable detect --json .               # machine-readable output
npx impeccable detect --github src/          # GitHub Actions annotations
npx impeccable detect --list-rules           # every rule with its id and description

Source files like JSX and TSX get the pattern rules only. Rules that need a rendered page, such as low contrast and tiny text, run when you scan a URL, so point the CLI at your dev server too: npx impeccable detect http://localhost:5173.

Exit code means findings, means a target couldn't be scanned. To allow your brand font everywhere, run npx impeccable ignores add-value overused-font Inter --reason "Brand font". To turn a rule off for one file, add a comment: <!-- impeccable-disable overused-font: exported brand doc -->. Run a detector scan · Configuration and ignores.

The installer detects your coding tools, asks whether to install for this project or globally, and offers the design hook where your tool supports one. Accept the hook. Reload your tool afterward. refreshes an existing install. For scripts, pass --providers=claude,codex,cursor and .

Three tools need one more step before the hook runs. In Codex, open and approve the project hook (again after an update that changes it). In Grok Build, run or launch with . In Hermes Agent, the hook is a plugin: run hermes plugins enable impeccable-design-hook once. Allow the hook in your harness.

Node is only needed for . The skill itself runs a self-contained engine binary that ships next to it or downloads once into .

Impeccable writes its working files under . A few are shared project artifacts and belong in the repo: , , , , and . Keep and in the repo too. The rest is screenshots, caches, and runtime state.

The folders that hold decision-round state (, .impeccable/mocks/worlds/) also ignore themselves. A can't untrack a file git already tracks; if you committed one earlier, run .

For new landing pages and showcase surfaces, Impeccable can generate a full-fidelity comp first and build to match it (bolder, slower), or build straight in code (leaner, faster). App screens and documents are always built in code. asks once and saves the answer as in ; the decision page lets you override it for one session. The choice only appears when your harness can generate images. Image generation · Configuration.

Hooks run outside model approval. In Claude Code, installed command hooks run even when you deny the model's own commands, so the first edit can download the engine. Review installed hooks before unattended runs, or pass --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' to turn them off for a run. The installer leaves hook entries it didn't add alone.

finds stale context files, unused settings, and broken hooks. Fix setup problems.

When a new design starts, the skill fetches a set of visual directions from the impeccable.style catalog. Turning telemetry off doesn't stop that request; it stops the anonymous record of which directions were shown and which one you picked, which is how the catalog learns what works. Your project name, files, code, and are never sent. Disable telemetry with npx impeccable telemetry off, , or in for the whole project. The full list of what is sent is on the privacy page.

  • Issues for bugs, questions, and ideas. Outside contributions start with an issue; see DEVELOP.md.
  • Follow @pbakaus for release notes and new rules.

items.title: Nutlope/hallmark
items.content:
Anti-AI-slop design skill for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

A design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode that refuses to look AI-generated.

usehallmark.com  ·  fifty themes  ·  custom on request  ·  redesign and audit by name

Hallmark holds a hard floor and then gets out of the way. It deals three themes from a catalog of fifty materials, builds the page around what the visitor came to do, and lints the result in a real browser against the tells that read as machine-made: the eyebrow above every heading, tracked-capital labels, one coloured word in a headline, a page of empty frames or nothing but photographs, a hero that misses its screen, an email sign-up at the end of every page, a form that says thanks without sending anything. A fresh-context reviewer gets the last word.

The gates come in tiers. The never ships (contrast, focus, reduced motion, invented facts, a broken phone layout). gates are the defaults a model falls into; a build with a reason may overrule one on the record. checks are craft detail that never blocks a ship.

  • Each is a material (paper, type, colour, surfaces, its own components and texture) with a picture of a finished page, and the build lays out its own page in it.
  • A booking page books, a shop sells, a newsletter subscribes: the action sits where the category puts it, and the page ends on it.
  • Ask for a custom page and Hallmark designs from your prompt alone, under the same rules and checks.
  • Point it at a URL, a dev server or an app and it captures the screenshots itself.
  • 755 openly licensed photos, picked per subject and credited on the page.
  • /hallmark redesign <path> rebuilds a page and keeps its content and wiring; only reports.

Ten of the fifty. A theme is a material, not a plan: it never says what a page contains or in what order, so two prompts in one theme make two different pages. Each is one file of at most 8 KB in with a picture beside it; a build reads exactly one. See them all at usehallmark.com.

Say and Hallmark drops the themes: no plan, no components, no palette recipe, only the floor, the gates and a short direction in to find one idea that only this client has and let it run the page.

  1. Pre-flight reads the project (fonts, palette, framework, a locked ) and asks once for the material: photos, screenshots, real numbers. Nothing is invented.
  2. offers three themes that fit the prompt and clear the log; deals the page's anatomy from its job.
  3. The hero is built alone, rendered and reviewed cold before the rest of the page exists.
  4. scripts/sloplint.mjs --render checks the page at eight widths, then a subagent reviews it with fresh eyes.

Each page is self-contained HTML and CSS, stamped in its first CSS comment with the decisions it took.

Hallmark never starts on a design that already exists unless you name it:

/hallmark redesign ./src/app
/hallmark audit ./index.html

A full redesign keeps the content and the wiring and changes the system and the layout; say for a restyle or for only the tells. records every link, field, handler and heading first, fails the redesign if one went missing, and the handoff is a side-by-side before and after.

npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g

installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (, screenshots) also need and Chrome; without them the static checks still run.

~/.claude/skills/hallmark or describe a new build
~/.agents/skills/hallmark or describe a new build
or describe a new build
or describe a new build
  • npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code (or , , , ).
  • /plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark, then /plugin install hallmark@hallmark (invoked as ).
  • node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs validates every theme and reference before it copies; adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code.
  • node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs <file-or-dir> --render.
  • If it does not fire on its own, name it: use hallmark to build ....

MIT. Use it, fork it, ship it.

The photo library (skills/hallmark/scripts/photos.json) lists photographs hosted on Wikimedia Commons and holds no image files. Each keeps its own licence (CC0, public domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA), and Hallmark credits every one it uses on the page. It does not use stock sites (Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay), whose terms bar AI tools from picking their images.

items.title: aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws
items.content:
Official, AWS-supported MCP servers, skills, and plugins to help AI agents build on AWS

Help AI coding agents build, deploy, and manage applications on AWS.

The Agent Toolkit for AWS gives AI coding agents the tools, knowledge, and guardrails they need to work with AWS services. It works with the coding agents developers already use — including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Kiro, and fx.

Use the Agent Toolkit directly from your terminal with the AWS CLI:

aws configure agent-toolkit

The plugins are available on the official Anthropic marketplace () which is added to your Claude Code installation by default. Use the following commands to install supported plugins from the toolkit:

For that covers service selection, CDK/CloudFormation, serverless, containers, storage, observability, billing, SDK usage, and deployment:

/plugin install aws-core@claude-plugins-official

If you get , update your local marketplace index first:

/plugin marketplace update claude-plugins-official

For that covers building AI agents on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore:

/plugin install aws-agents@claude-plugins-official

For that covers data lake, analytics, and ETL workflows with S3 Tables, AWS Glue, and Athena:

/plugin install aws-data-analytics@claude-plugins-official

For used to investigate incidents, review code and execute UAT for release readiness, scan code for vulnerabilities, and run penetration tests with AWS DevOps Agent and AWS Security Agent.

/plugin marketplace add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws
/plugin install aws-agents-for-devsecops
/reload-plugins

# Or from Claude's official marketplace:
/plugin install aws-agents-for-devsecops@claude-plugins-official
/reload-plugins

# Setup:
/aws-agents-for-devsecops:setup

For that covers startup-focused architecture, cost, security, and AWS Activate guidance, plus migrations to AWS from Azure, GCP, Heroku, and AI stacks such as OpenAI and Gemini, install from this repository's marketplace:

/plugin marketplace add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws
/plugin install aws-startup-advisor@agent-toolkit-for-aws
/reload-plugins

codex plugin marketplace add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws

Then launch Codex and run to browse and install the plugin.

Add this repository as a team marketplace from Settings → Plugins → Team Marketplaces → Add Marketplace → Import from Repo, pointing it at aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws. Cursor indexes the plugins listed in .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json on import.

Then open the panel and install the plugin (start here), or and as needed. Each plugin bundles the AWS MCP Server configuration and agent skills.

devin plugins install aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws#plugins/aws-core

This requires and adds the plugin to your personal plugins, so it also loads in Devin cloud sessions and Devin Desktop. Add to install on this machine only. To install a different plugin, replace with its name from Plugins, such as or .

In the Devin web app, choose Customize → Plugins → Add plugin → From repository, enter aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws, and set the subdirectory to (or another plugin's directory). Personal plugins added there are also available in the Devin CLI and Devin Desktop.

Kiro setup has two independent parts: the AWS MCP Server (for runtime AWS API access and documentation search) and local skills (for task-specific agent guidance). They complement each other but work independently — skills don't require the MCP server, and the MCP server doesn't serve locally-installed skills.

1. Add the AWS MCP Server to your Kiro MCP configuration ():

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "aws": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "mcp-proxy-for-aws-cli@latest",
        "https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp",
        "--metadata",
        "AWS_REGION=us-west-2"
      ]
    }
  }
}

The MCP server gives your agent access to AWS APIs, sandboxed script execution, and real-time documentation search.

from this repository:

npx skills add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/skills

This installs skill files to (global) or (project-level). Each skill is a directory containing a file and optionally a subdirectory with additional context the agent reads from the local filesystem when needed. Kiro discovers installed skills automatically and activates them on demand when a task matches.

You need uv installed. An AWS account with credentials configured locally is required for API calls and script execution, but not for documentation search or skill discovery. See the user guide for detailed setup instructions.

fx setup has the same two independent parts as Kiro: the AWS MCP Server (for runtime AWS API access and documentation search) and local skills (for task-specific agent guidance). Skills don't require the MCP server, and the MCP server doesn't serve locally-installed skills.

1. Add the AWS MCP Server from your terminal. fx stores MCP servers in , so the server is available in every project:

fx mcp add aws uvx mcp-proxy-for-aws-cli@latest https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp --metadata AWS_REGION=us-west-2

Or add it to by hand. fx uses the key rather than , to select the transport, and a single array holding the executable and its arguments:

{
  "mcp": {
    "aws": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": [
        "uvx",
        "mcp-proxy-for-aws-cli@latest",
        "https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp",
        "--metadata",
        "AWS_REGION=us-west-2"
      ]
    }
  }
}

If a session is already open when you edit the file, run to pick up the change. The MCP server gives your agent access to AWS APIs, sandboxed script execution, and real-time documentation search.

from this repository:

npx skills add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/skills -a fx

This installs skill files to (project-level); add to install to (global). fx also discovers skills already installed for other agents in , , and , so a project set up for Codex or Claude Code needs no second copy. Each skill is a directory containing a file and optionally a subdirectory with additional context the agent reads from the local filesystem when needed. fx reads skill metadata at startup and loads a skill's instructions when you or the agent invokes it; type in the composer or run to browse what's installed.

You need uv installed. An AWS account with credentials configured locally is required for API calls and script execution, but not for documentation search or skill discovery. See the user guide for detailed setup instructions.

Then install skills from this repository:

npx skills add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/skills

You need uv installed. An AWS account with credentials configured locally is required for API calls and script execution, but not for documentation search or skill discovery. See the user guide for detailed setup instructions.

Plugins bundle the AWS MCP Server configuration and agent skills into a single install for your coding agent.

Core AWS skills and MCP Server configuration. Covers service selection, CDK/CloudFormation, serverless, containers, storage, observability, billing, SDK usage, and deployment.
Skills for building AI agents on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore.
Skills for data lake, analytics, and ETL workflows with S3 Tables, AWS Glue, and Athena.
Puts an AWS Startups Solutions Architect in your coding assistant. Recommends the smallest architecture for your stage, credits, and team, then can scaffold it, migrate you from Azure, Google Cloud, or Heroku, move model calls to Amazon Bedrock, investigate production incidents, answer AWS Activate credits eligibility questions, and find startup offers you can use.

Plugins are currently available for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Devin. For other agents, configure the AWS MCP Server directly and install skills from this repository.

Agent skills are curated packages of instructions and reference materials that help agents complete specific AWS tasks. Skills are loaded on demand — agents discover and retrieve only what's relevant to the current task.

npx skills add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/skills

Browse the directory to see all available skills.

Recommended project-level configuration files that tell agents how to use AWS most effectively — for example, by using the AWS MCP Server, discovering available skills, or searching documentation before acting.

The AWS MCP Server is a managed server that gives agents access to AWS through the Model Context Protocol. It provides:

  • — Interact with any of the 300+ AWS services through a single authenticated endpoint.
  • Sandboxed script execution — Agents can run Python scripts in an isolated environment for complex multi-step operations.
  • Real-time documentation access — Search and retrieve current AWS documentation, API references, and service capabilities without authentication.
  • — Amazon CloudWatch metrics, IAM context keys for agent-specific policies, and AWS CloudTrail audit logging.

How the Agent Toolkit relates to the MCP servers, skills, and plugins in AWS Labs

In 2025, AWS began releasing MCP servers, skills, and plugins as part of AWS Labs. The Agent Toolkit for AWS is the successor to those tools. We recommend using the Agent Toolkit for AWS, because it offers key features including:

  • IAM condition keys that distinguish between agent actions and human actions, so you can write policies that apply only to agents. For example, you can write policies that only allow read-only actions through the MCP server, even if the user’s underlying IAM role can take write actions).
  • CloudWatch metrics and CloudTrail audit logging for every request, so you can monitor and audit coding agent activity.
  • Agent skills that have undergone thorough end-to-end evaluations, so you can be confident that workflows will complete successfully.

AWS Labs MCP servers, skills, and plugins will continue to work and accept contributions, and over time the best of AWS Labs will be transitioned to the Agent Toolkit for AWS to ensure that customers can access the broadest array of tooling and guidance for their agents.

items.content:
Node.js JavaScript runtime ✨🐢🚀✨

Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment.

Contributors are expected to act in a collaborative manner to move the project forward. We encourage the constructive exchange of contrary opinions and compromise. The TSC reserves the right to limit or block contributors who repeatedly act in ways that discourage, exhaust, or otherwise negatively affect other participants.

  • : Under active development where semver-major changes are allowed. Each October, a new release line (for example, Node.js 27) branches off and receives Alpha releases (for example, ) for 6 months, then are promoted to Current (see below) each April. Alpha releases are signed, tagged, and tested through CITGM, but their API and ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use.
  • : Under active development, no semver-major changes allowed. Node.js releases a new major version once a year, in April. Releases stay Current for 6 months, then convert to LTS (see below) each October. Their ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use.
  • : Releases under Long Term Support, with a focus on stability and security. Only changes that have been on Alpha or Current release for two weeks can be backported to a typical LTS release. Every major version becomes an LTS release, and receives 30 months of LTS support, for a total of 36 months from its first Current release to End-of-Life. LTS release lines have alphabetically-ordered code names, beginning with Node.js 4 Argon.
  • : Code from the branch built every 24-hours when there are changes. Unlike Alpha releases, nightly builds are automated and untested. Use with caution.

Release lines up to and including Node.js 26 follow the previous schedule, where a new major version was released every 6 months and only even-numbered major versions became LTS. See the Node.js release schedule announcement for details.

The latest directory is an alias for the latest Current release. The latest- directory is an alias for the latest release from an LTS line. For example, the latest-hydrogen directory contains the latest Hydrogen (Node.js 18) release.

Each directory and filename includes the version (e.g., ), followed by the UTC date (e.g., for April 24, 2024), and the short commit SHA of the HEAD of the release (e.g., ). For instance, a full directory name might look like v22.0.0-nightly20240424ddd0a9e494.

Download directories contain a file with SHA checksums for the files and the releaser PGP signature.

You can get a trusted keyring from nodejs/release-keys, e.g. using :

curl -fsLo "/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" "https://github.com/nodejs/release-keys/raw/HEAD/gpg/pubring.kbx"

Alternatively, you can import the releaser keys in your default keyring, see Release keys for commands on how to do that.

Then, you can verify the files you've downloaded locally (if you're using your default keyring, pass --keyring="${GNUPGHOME:-~/.gnupg}/pubring.kbx"):

curl -fsO "https://nodejs.org/dist/${VERSION}/SHASUMS256.txt.asc" \
&& gpgv --keyring="/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" --output SHASUMS256.txt < SHASUMS256.txt.asc \
&& shasum --check SHASUMS256.txt --ignore-missing

See BUILDING.md for instructions on how to build Node.js from source and a list of supported platforms.

For information on reporting security vulnerabilities in Node.js, see SECURITY.md.
